title: Mapping the Sea Floor
objective: After this level you can explain how sonar mapped the ocean floor.
summary: Light can't reach the deep floor, so it's mapped with sound: first lead lines, then sonar echoes from the 1920s and multibeam fans from the 1960s. As of April 2026, 28.7% was mapped.

cards.headline: We have better maps of Mars than of the floor of our own ocean.
cards.body: That's the U.S. Geological Survey's verdict. The reason: light can't get through deep seawater, so the tools that map land from above can't see the bottom. So how do you map a floor you can't see? You listen for it.

cards.headline: One rope, one number
cards.body: In the early 1800s, sailors measured depth with a lead line: a weighted rope lowered over the side until it hit bottom. Each drop gave the depth at a single point, so charting even a harbor was slow, laborious work. Now remember Level 2: the ocean averages about 3,700 m deep. Mapping a whole ocean floor one rope at a time was never going to happen.

cards.headline: Ping, then wait
cards.body: Sonar, developed in the 1920s, swapped the rope for sound. A ship sends a sound down and times how long its echo takes to bounce back off the bottom: the longer the wait, the deeper the floor. It works where light fails because sound travels far through seawater. Remember Level 8: no sunlight at all reaches below 1,000 m. The deep floor gets mapped by ear, not by eye.

mascot.line: Next time you hear an echo, you're doing a tiny bit of oceanography.

cards.headline: A fan of sound, and a deadline
cards.body: In the 1960s came multibeam sonar: many beams of sound at once, fanned out to map a wide strip under the ship and out to each side. Even so, when the Seabed 2030 project launched in 2017, only about 6% of the ocean floor had been mapped in modern detail. By April 2026, it had reached 28.7%. The goal is all of it by 2030. That's a lot of lawn left to mow.
cards.callout: 2017: about 6% · April 2026: 28.7% · Goal: all of it by 2030

questions.prompt: As of April 2026, how much of the world's ocean floor had the Seabed 2030 project counted as mapped in modern detail?

options.label: About 6%
options.rationale: That was the figure when the project launched in 2017.

options.label: About 71%
options.rationale: That's the share of Earth's surface covered by water.

options.label: About 97%
options.rationale: That's the share of Earth's water held in the ocean.

questions.explanation: Seabed 2030 reported 28.7% of the ocean floor mapped as of April 2026, up from about 6% in 2017.

questions.prompt: How does a ship's sonar work out the depth of the sea floor below it?

options.label: It photographs the bottom with bright lamps
options.rationale: Light can't get through that much water.

options.label: It times how long a sound's echo takes to return
It lowers a weighted rope until it hits bottom
options.rationale: That's the old lead line that sonar replaced.

options.label: It measures how salty the deepest water is
options.rationale: Salt has nothing to do with sonar depth.

questions.explanation: Sonar sends a sound down and times its echo off the bottom: the longer the wait, the deeper the floor.

questions.prompt: From Level 8: no sunlight reaches below 1,000 m. How does that help explain why Mars is better mapped than our own sea floor?

options.label: Mars is closer to Earth than the deep sea floor is
options.rationale: Mars is millions of kilometers away.

options.label: The deep floor is too hot for cameras to work
options.rationale: Heat isn't the problem; darkness is.

options.label: Light can't reach the deep floor, so maps must use sound
Sonar was invented only after Mars was mapped

questions.explanation: Light can't get through deep seawater, so the tools that map land from above can't see the bottom; sound can.
